subject: Abundance estimates will not stop increasing with increasing K

messages.author: 9839c75e5703f57c
messages.subject: Abundance estimates will not stop increasing with increasing K
parts:
Dear unmarked users,

I am estimating the abundance of salamander larvae over a timespan of 11 weeks in five streams, with each stream having 30 pools (but I analyse these streams separately). 
For this I collected replicated count data.

The following is an analysis of one stream with 30 pools ("30 sites").

My Null model is the following:
pcountOpen(~1, ~1, ~1, ~1, umf1, K=t, se = FALSE, dynamics = ("trend"),
                  immigration = TRUE, mixture = "NB", control = list(trace = T, REPORT = 1))



To find K I wrote a loop, that loops through different K's.
It generates an Abundance list, as well as a list of the different K's with their AIC values.
Then I summed up all estimates from one model (Abun_sum). 

Here is what I coded for the loop:

ks <- seq(150, 5*Kmin, Kmin/2) #Kmin = 54 (the highest value ever observed)
Abun <- numeric(0)
AIC_list <- matrix(0, ncol = 2)
colnames(AIC_list) <- c("K", "AIC")
for(t in ks) {
  m <- pcountOpen(~1, ~1, ~1, ~1, umf1, K=t, se = FALSE, dynamics = ("trend"),
                  immigration = TRUE, mixture = "NB", control = list(trace = T, REPORT = 1))
  r <- ranef(m)
  a <- bup(r)
  Abun <- rbind(Abun, a)
  #isolate AIC value of model m
  K_AIC <- cbind("K" = t, "AIC" = m@AIC)
  AIC_list <- rbind(AIC_list, K_AIC)
}

#sum up all estimates from one model
j = 1
seq <- seq(30, 30*length(ks), by = 30)
Abun_s <- numeric(0)

for (i in seq){
  Abun_sum <- sum(Abun[j:i,])
  Abun_s <- rbind(Abun_s, Abun_sum)
  j = j + 30
}


This is the output of the AIC_list and the sums:
> AIC_list
       K      AIC
[1,]   0    0.000
[2,] 150 3252.709
[3,] 177 3242.215
[4,] 204 3234.455
[5,] 231 3228.494
[6,] 258 3223.826

> Abun_s
              [,1]
Abun_sum  8401.331
Abun_sum  9790.081
Abun_sum 11185.994
Abun_sum 12574.747
Abun_sum 13949.482

If I plot it it looks like this:



Then I tried to increase K even more...
And with the same model and code I got the following output:

> AIC_list
       K      AIC
[1,]   0    0.000
[2,] 260 3223.522
[3,] 270 3222.079
[4,] 280 3220.754
[5,] 290 3219.537
[6,] 300 3218.420
[7,] 310 3217.393

But with sums of:
> Abun_s
                   [,1]
Abun_sum 14050.63
Abun_sum 14554.98
Abun_sum 15056.67
Abun_sum 15555.63
Abun_sum 16051.78
Abun_sum 16544.85



This overall sum of abundance estimates should stabilise somewhen with an increasing K. But this doesn't seem to be the case here.
(1) Does someone know why the abundance estimates won't stop increasing?
(2) Also, there is an increase in the second Abun_s output of 500 in each step. But the AIC value is decreasing by ca 1... This seems odd to me as well.


I don't know where to look anymore. I also checked my raw data and my unmarkedFram - everything seems to be fine.
This code worked fine with the other streams, but not with this one.




All thoughts are greatly appreciated!

Best,
Michelle

parts:
Hi Michelle,

maybe K needs to be even higher? :-) Do you have any reasons to think that K should be lower? What is the detectability in the model with the highest K?
Could you do perhaps something like summary(m) and send it?

Tomas

parts:
Hi Tomas,

thank you for your response!
Well, in the other streams my K's are:
K = 295 with Kmin = 131
K = 126 with Kmin = 23
K = 242 with Kmin = 44
K = 152 with Kmin = 61
I know K also depends on the detection probability, but since I observed all streams in the same manner there should not be so much of a difference, right?
Furthermore, I also tried it with K = 400, and the pattern stays the same. It still is a linear increase... and it doesn't seem to stabilize.

I don't think K should be higher than 300, because with K = 300, the sum of the estimates is equal to 16051.78. For a comparison, it is around 7500 in the stream with the highest K (K=295 and the most larvae found)  and around 5700 in a stream with comparable amount of larvae in it (K=242 and Kmin=44). It is furthermore rather unlikely to find 16 thousand larvae over a time span of 11 weeks in such small pools. So even if it was right and the model needs such a high K, it would not make sense biologically.
The detection probability is 0.169428, which is rather low...
I'm not sure if my only option is to run the models with even higher K's?
And do you know how the AIC can decrease very slowly (by 1) with the a linear increase of estimates (~500 individuals)? This shouldn't be the case either, am I right?

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Abundance estimates will not stop increasing with increasing K
parts:
Hi Michelle,

It's also possible that the model just isn't a good fit to your dataset, at least for the stream in question (or not enough data) and the result is optimization problems that mean no realistic value of K is likely to work. These open population models can be pretty hard to get working. It might help me (or, more likely, others who know these models better than me) to understand why you chose the 'trend' model and immigration=TRUE in your specific case (biologically speaking). Have you tried other variations? It also might be useful to see a sample of the data from the stream that is causing issues, and perhaps from one where the model seems to work.

Finally, it would be useful to see what kind of SE estimates you are getting if you set se=TRUE, even if K is too low.

I wouldn't necessarily expect there to be much of a relationship between the estimated AIC and estimated abundance.

Ken

parts:
Hi Michelle,

agree with Ken. These models are hard to fit. They have certain assumptions, like the closure assumption, i.e. the population doesn't change between corresponding visits. And, if there is any variation between the visits due to other factors than the detectability, this between-visit variation will be erroneously explained by the N-mixture model as low detectability, so it will bias your detectability downwards... Might help if you add covariates for the detectability, if there are some reasonable ones, but the model might be even harder to fit then.

Also, you assume that these abundance values are too large, but ... sometimes it might not be the case. We had such experience in our Atlas, when we came to densities sometimes notably larger than those already published. And our conclusion was (with some support from experts) that the majority previous estimates in literature were underestimated because they didn't consider detectability properly. Of couse might not be your case but just to share our experience.

Anyway, with the results you've shown, I would definitely try to raise K until it stabilizes, just to see where it goes. Let it run over the weekend :-)

Best regards

Tomas
On Fri, 6 Nov 2020 at 18:59, Ken Kellner <ken.k...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Michelle,

It's also possible that the model just isn't a good fit to your dataset, at least for the stream in question (or not enough data) and the result is optimization problems that mean no realistic value of K is likely to work. These open population models can be pretty hard to get working. It might help me (or, more likely, others who know these models better than me) to understand why you chose the 'trend' model and immigration=TRUE in your specific case (biologically speaking). Have you tried other variations? It also might be useful to see a sample of the data from the stream that is causing issues, and perhaps from one where the model seems to work.

Finally, it would be useful to see what kind of SE estimates you are getting if you set se=TRUE, even if K is too low.

I wouldn't necessarily expect there to be much of a relationship between the estimated AIC and estimated abundance.

Ken

I chose the trend model, because I don't want to model the recruitment term.
I only look at count data of salamander larvae in the water and I do not look at the adults. Since the larvae cannot reproduce and recruit new individuals, I did not want to include this recruitment term.
